The rot-wood shrivels from the light like a hand from a stove, and crumbles into wet black ash.
The sap makes the moss burn longer. Nana's book was right about everything.
Nana's book is always right.
Don't tell her. She'll be unbearable.
On the drowned altar, half-buried in silt, something glints. A plain copper ring.
Inside the band, worn nearly smooth: _T. — always the long way home._
Tobin Pell's ring. She'll want this back.
Someone's wedding ring. Someone in Mirefen might know whose.
The black pool is perfectly still. Bones ring its shore — fish, birds, something larger.
In the middle of the water, bubbles rise. Slowly. Like breathing.
I want it on record that I said "who wants to go first" and meant it rhetorically.
The pool heaves. Something rises out of it — a bloated, eyeless thing of black mud and gristle, ringed with mouths.
That's it. That's the rot. That's what's in her lungs.
Then let's get it out.
When it is over, Ilse wades into the shallows with her knife and her jaw set, and comes back with something black and dense in a jar.
Rot-gall. The sickness, made solid.
You just — you just stuck your whole arm in that.
It was in Mother Osk's lungs. My arm can cope.
We killed the thing in the black pool. Ilse cut its heart out and put it in a jar. I have never been so proud of anyone, or so glad she's on my side.
Ilse works for an hour without speaking. Moss, sap, gall — ground, steeped, strained. The Lantern fills with the smell of it.
Smells like a boot.
Like a boot that drowned and came back angry.
Thank you both. Hold her head, Doctor.
Ilse tips the draught between the old woman's lips, a spoonful at a time. Nobody breathes.
Under Osk's skin, the black veins tremble — and begin, very slowly, to fade.
...Who in the name of every frog in the fen fed me a _boot_?
Mother Osk!
Hesk. You look terrible. Have you been making soup again? I can smell it from here.
Daft heron.
You. Girl. You did this.
With help.
Your hands didn't shake.
They did. You just couldn't see.
That's the whole trick of it, girl.
And you're Ysolde's. I thought I dreamed you.
You called me by her name.
I've known your mother since she was smaller than that scruffy one.
Came to every Keepers' Conclave with her nose in a book. Just like you, I expect.
Osk turns her head toward the brass cradle at the heart of the room. It is empty. She looks at it for a long time.
Hesk. Where's my stone.
They took it.
The Choir. The night your fever broke out. They had the Hierophant's seal. They said the Gloam was rising, that the stone was safer in the Cathedral, that they'd harmonize it and bring it home—
And you were saying "take it, take it, it's too heavy"—
I was talking about the _blanket_, you great soggy heron.
...It's not your fault, boy. I'd told him no twice. To his face.
They didn't come for safekeeping. They came because I was too sick to say it a third time.
He wanted my stone. Said he needed all seven for something. A "harmony," he called it. He sent me one of those last spring.
Her eyes have gone to Wren's pack. Wren takes out the case of forks.
Put that away. I can hear it from here.
I threw mine in the bog. Then the rot came up out of the bog. Make of that what you like.
It sings to the others. All the forks, everywhere. They are waiting for something.
...Well. Aren't you a strange one. Come here, child. Let me see your face.
_(very quietly)_ Oh, Cassian. What have you done.
Do you know who I am?
I know who you look like. That isn't the same thing.
And it isn't my story to tell. I wasn't there.
Go to Elowen. In Verdance, at the heart of the Thornwood. She's older than dirt and twice as honest — and she was in Aurenne the night the city went dark.
The night the city went — what?
Ask Elowen.
And tell her Osk says she still owes me a goose.
